title.en: GRPO: Clipping The Update So One Good Sample Can't Wreck It

description.en: grpo_group_advantage turned each sampled completion's reward into an advantage. On its own, a big advantage times a big probability ratio can push the policy too far in one step. GRPO borrows PPO's clipped surrogate objective to cap how much any single completion is allowed to move the policy.

story_variants.en:
## An Advantage Alone Is Not Safe To Optimize

"`A = 1.4017` says the top completion from last lesson deserves a strong push," Vaathiyaar says. "But if you multiply that advantage straight through by how much the policy's probability for that completion has already shifted, one lucky sample can drag the whole policy off a cliff in a single update. PPO's fix -- which GRPO reuses directly -- is to clip how far that push is allowed to go."

### The Probability Ratio

First, measure how much the *new* policy's probability for a completion has moved versus the policy that generated it:

> **ratio = pi_new(y|x) / pi_old(y|x)**

`ratio = 1` means nothing has changed yet. `ratio = 1.35` means the new policy is 35% more likely to produce this completion than the one that sampled it.

### The Clipped Surrogate

GRPO's per-completion objective takes the smaller of the raw push and a clipped version of it:

> **surrogate = min(ratio x A, clip(ratio, 1-eps, 1+eps) x A)**

With `eps = 0.2`, `ratio` is clamped to `[0.8, 1.2]` before the second term is computed. Take the best completion from last lesson, `A = 1.4017`, with `ratio = 1.35`:

```
unclipped = 1.35 * 1.4017 = 1.8923
clipped_ratio = min(1.2, max(0.8, 1.35)) = 1.2
clipped = 1.2 * 1.4017 = 1.6820
surrogate = min(1.8923, 1.6820) = 1.6820
```

The clip wins -- the update is capped at what a `20%` probability shift would have given, even though the ratio actually moved further than that.

> **Vaathiyaar's rule:** when the advantage is positive, `min` picks whichever term is *smaller*, which caps runaway growth. When the advantage is negative, the same `min` call caps runaway shrinkage instead -- the clip protects against overreacting in both directions, not just one. That symmetry is why the same one-line formula covers 'this sample was great, don't overreact' and 'this sample was bad, don't overreact' with no special-casing.

Today you implement the clipped surrogate for one completion, then average it across a whole group.

q.en: Why does GRPO clip the probability ratio instead of optimizing ratio x A directly?

en: To make every advantage positive before optimizing
Because the ratio can't be computed without clipping
To speed up training by skipping low-reward samples
So one lucky sample can't push the policy too far in one step

uth_example:
eps = 0.2
samples = [                     # (probability ratio new/old, advantage)
    (1.05, 1.4),                # small step on a good sample
    (1.60, 1.4),                # big jump on a good sample -> clipped
    (0.50, -0.9),               # big drop on a bad sample -> clipped
    (0.95, -0.9),
]

rows = []
for ratio, adv in samples:
    unclipped = ratio * adv
    clipped = max(1 - eps, min(1 + eps, ratio)) * adv
    rows.append({"ratio": ratio, "adv": adv, "objective": round(min(unclipped, clipped), 3),
                 "was_clipped": clipped < unclipped})

for r in rows:
    print(r)
print("group objective:", round(sum(r["objective"] for r in rows) / len(rows), 3))

under_the_hood.summary: GRPO multiplies each completion's advantage by the probability ratio pi_new / pi_old, but also computes the ratio clipped to [1 - eps, 1 + eps] and takes the smaller of the two products, so one update cannot move the policy too far on any sample.

steps.title: The probability ratio
steps.body: ratio = pi_new(y|x) / pi_old(y|x), computed per token as exp(new log-prob - old log-prob). 1.0 means unchanged; 1.35 means the update made this completion 35% more likely than the policy that sampled it.

steps.title: The unclipped push
steps.body: ratio x A rewards making high-advantage completions more likely. With ratio 1.35 and A = 1.4017 that is 1.8923, and nothing stops the optimiser from pushing the ratio far higher on a lucky sample.

steps.title: Clip, then take the minimum
steps.body: With eps = 0.2 the ratio is clipped to 1.2, giving 1.2 x 1.4017 = 1.6820. The surrogate is min(1.8923, 1.6820) = 1.6820. Once the ratio passes 1.2, further increases earn nothing, so their gradient is zero.

steps.title: It works in both directions
steps.body: For a negative advantage the minimum picks the more pessimistic term, so the policy cannot gain by pushing a bad completion's probability far below 1 - eps either. Clipping limits step size, whatever the sign.

steps.title: Average over the group
steps.body: The objective averages the per-token surrogates over all completions in the group (and over prompts), then gradient ascent maximises it. This is PPO's clipping, reused unchanged; GRPO only changed where the advantage comes from.

under_the_hood.takeaway: Clipping turns 'push toward good samples' into 'push, but only a little per update'. It is what keeps policy-gradient training stable when a few samples have large advantages.
